This page runs no code. It says why a tuned model's own score is not an
estimate, which quantity the nested number is, how to read the standard
error beside it, why the outer folds disagree, and when nesting is worth its
cost. The worked example is `vignette("nested-cv")`.

## The case for nesting

Tuning by cross-validation scores every candidate on the same resamples and
keeps the one that scored best. The best of a set of noisy numbers is biased
upward, so the winner's score carries the selection along with it and
overstates what the model will do on new data, by an amount nothing in the
output reveals. At a small sample size the bias is small next to resampling
noise, so the number is not reliably better-looking either; the structural
argument is the reason to distrust it, not its sign. That is why the results
object and the final fit both refuse tune's ranking generics such as
`show_best()`.

Nested cross-validation puts the whole tune-and-fit procedure inside a
second, outer resampling loop. Each outer fold tunes from scratch on its own
analysis rows, fits the winner there, and scores it once on assessment rows
the tuning never saw. The mean of those outer scores is the estimate.

The number `collect_metrics()` reports describes the whole tune-and-fit
procedure: resample, tune, select, fit. That is the number to report. The
model fitted at the end for deployment is a separate object, and it has no
performance number of its own, because everything computable from its
training data was used up in selecting and fitting it.

## The quantity estimated

The estimate is of the k-fold test error of the tune-and-fit procedure
(Bayle et al., 2026): the error of resampling, tuning, selecting and
fitting, on the particular analysis sets these folds drew, then predicting
fresh data drawn like the training data.

Two quantities it is not. It is not the risk of the deployed model, which is
built afterwards on all the rows and whose own error nothing in a nested run
estimates. And it is not the same quantity averaged over training sets,
which is usually what a reader has in mind: Luo and Barber (2026) prove that
any assumption-free test of it needs a dataset many times larger than the
training size, so this package offers no test of it. Nor is it a claim about the parameter values the deployed model
carries, or about a different population or sample size.

## A slight pessimism

The number tends to look a little worse than the procedure deserves. Every
outer fold trains on its analysis rows only, so every model scored is built
on less data than the model finally deployed, and less data usually means
worse predictions. Varma and Simon (2006) separate this training-size component, whose sign can go either way,
from the selection-driven component, which is always optimistic.

Two measurements give a sense of the size. Varma and Simon (2006) found a
nested estimate of 54.2% against a true 50.0% on null data with 40 samples,
a 4.2-point overshoot they attribute to training on 39 rows rather than 40.
Wilimitis and Walsh (2023), on 41,121 hospital visits, found nested
cross-validation among the most pessimistic methods they compared, by
roughly 1 to 2% of AUROC and 5 to 9% of AUPR against a held-out benchmark,
though the same study reports a cell where the nested estimate came out
optimistic instead.

The gap is a property of the estimator, not a prediction about any one run,
and never a licence to adjust the reported figure upward.

## The standard error

`std_err` is the standard error of the mean across the outer folds: the
standard deviation of the fold scores divided by the square root of their
number. It is not the fold-to-fold spread, which is larger by that factor,
and quoting it as though it described the folds understates their
disagreement; `collect_metrics(res, summarize = FALSE)` gives the per-fold
scores. It is also not a confidence interval. This package ships no inference on the
nested estimate.

## Comparing two workflows

If the loop is run on two workflows and one comes back lower, nothing in the
output says whether the difference is real, because there is no valid
interval here to subtract. Bayle et al. (2026) give a sharper reason not to
reach for one: the stability condition that makes a single procedure's
cross-validation interval valid can fail for the difference between two
procedures even when it holds for each, and it fails hardest when the two
are similar. A gap
between two nested estimates is a reason to look closer, never a result.

The same covers a set of workflows run through one design with
`nested_workflow_map()`. Picking the workflow with the best estimate is a
selection step the outer loop did not nest, so the package registers no
ranking or best-workflow method for the set, and the chosen workflow's
estimate is what a comparison read, never what choosing it achieves.

## Disagreement between folds

The results object keeps every fold's choice. When the folds split over a parameter, the data does not
pick its value clearly, so whichever value the final model carries was not
strongly preferred by the evidence. That is not a defect in the estimate,
which already averages over this variability. It is a defect in any story
about the selected parameters being the right ones.

Disagreement is expected wherever the candidates perform about equally well:
as two candidates' predictions converge, which of them wins any particular
fold becomes close to a coin flip (Bayle et al., 2026).

## The cost of nesting

What decides whether nesting pays is how much room the selection step had to
overfit. It removes most when the search is large relative to the data. Tibshirani
and Tibshirani (2009) found the optimism of a tuned cross-validation score
material only when the features vastly outnumber the observations: under 3
points on pure noise with 400 observations and 100 features, against a
minimum error rate of 0.384 for a true 0.5 with 40 observations and 1000
features. Wide data, a big grid, and a preprocessing step the loop has to
redo are where the bias is largest.

It removes little when the data is tall and the search is small. Wilimitis
and Walsh (2023) ran that case, 41,121 visits and a modest grid, and nesting
bought nothing but the pessimism above at a cost that grew quadratically in
the fold count. Their recommendation, and this package's, is to nest when
the feature space is wide relative to the sample, when many algorithms and
parameters are in play, and when the compute is affordable.

Small data is not fine without it. Vabalas et al. (2019) simulated pure
noise, where the honest accuracy is 50%, and found flat cross-validation
still reporting better than chance at a sample size of 1000, while nested
cross-validation was indistinguishable from chance at 96.5% of the sample
sizes tested. The bias thins with sample size and does not disappear.

## Feature selection inside the workflow

Vabalas et al. (2019) also compared leaving feature selection outside the
loop against leaving parameter tuning outside it, and the first was far more
damaging. This package orchestrates tuning, so a pipeline that selects
features must put that step in the recipe inside the workflow it hands over.
Everything in the workflow is re-estimated inside every fold. Anything done
to the data before the call is not, and no result here can tell that it
happened.
